The Dickcissel Spiza americana is a migratory emberizid finch of North American grasslands whose life history measurements reflect a fast-paced reproductive strategy typical of temperate-zone passerines. At the standard avian body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], incubation proceeds rapidly, and the age at hatching is just 12 days [ab = 12 days] when eggs are maintained at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a thermal optimum characteristic of ground-nesting species. Hatchling wet weight at birth averages 2.80 grams [Wwb = averages 2.80 grams], a value consistent with the altricial mode of development in small songbirds, where neonates emerge nearly naked and entirely dependent on parental brooding and provisioning. This initial mass is remarkably close to the wet weight of a freshly laid egg, which in this species is approximately 2.75 grams [Ww0 = approximately 2.75 grams], indicating that the embryo converts the majority of the egg's content into body tissue before hatching. The relationship between initial egg mass and hatchling mass is typical of birds that produce single-brood clutches in a highly seasonal environment.

Under the same thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] that drives metabolic processes during the active season, fledging occurs at 10.25 days after hatching [tx = 10.25 days after hatching], a developmental milestone characterized by the chick leaving the nest for the first time. This rapid fledging period is among the shortest recorded for passerines of comparable adult body mass and has been linked to the species' reliance on ephemeral tallgrass prairie habitats that impose a narrow window for breeding. Field observations indicate that young birds reach the fledgling stage with a body mass only a fraction of the adult asymptotic weight, underscoring the importance of continued parental food delivery after nest departure. The ecological consequences of this early nest exodus include elevated juvenile mortality during the first week of independence, but the strategy reduces the risk of entire brood loss to nest predators such as snakes and ground squirrels.

Sexual maturation in the Dickcissel proceeds rapidly under the warm temperatures of the late spring breeding grounds, with puberty attained at 30.75 days after hatching [tp = 30.75 days after hatching] when birds are maintained at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This remarkably short interval between hatching and gonadal maturation is unusual among North American emberizids and may represent an adaptation to the species' extended north-south migration corridor, which compresses the available breeding period at higher latitudes. First reproduction, or the initiation of the first brood, typically occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] at the same standard body temperature of 41.6 °C, meaning that most individuals do not breed until their second calendar year at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The delayed onset of breeding relative to puberty has been interpreted as a bet-hedging strategy, allowing young birds to accumulate sufficient body condition and territory experience before investing in offspring.

Adult body mass in the Dickcissel shows pronounced sexual dimorphism, a trait that has implications for both reproductive success and survival. The ultimate wet weight for females, representing the asymptotic adult mass, averages 25.2 grams [Wwi = 25.2 grams], whereas males reach a significantly greater ultimate wet weight of 28.5 grams [Wwi = 28.5 grams], a difference of roughly 13 percent. This dimorphism is correlated with the species' polygynous mating system, in which heavier males defend larger territories and attract more females to nest within their boundaries. Ecological studies have demonstrated that male body mass peaks during the early breeding season and declines progressively through the summer as the demands of territory defense and vocal advertisement take a toll on energy reserves. The adult mass values reported here fall within the typical range for a sparrow-sized passerine but at the upper end for grassland specialists that rely on seed-based diets during the non-breeding season.

Maximum lifespan in the Dickcissel has been estimated from long-term banding returns and recapture records at 4.8 years [am = 4.8 years] under field conditions at a standard body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], making this species relatively short-lived compared to other emberizids of similar size. Reproductive output during the breeding season is moderate but concentrated within a brief interval: females produce 2 to 6 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 to 6 eggs per clutch], with approximately 1.75 clutches annually [F_R_i = approximately 1.75 clutches annually]. This annual reproductive schedule yields a maximum of roughly 10 eggs per year per female, a figure that is constrained by the length of the breeding season and the energetic demands of molt and pre-migratory fat deposition. Brood parasitism by the Brown-headed Cowbird Molothrus ater further reduces realized fecundity in many populations, particularly in fragmented prairie landscapes where host detection is higher. The combination of rapid development, modest adult lifespan, and sustained reproductive effort defines the Dickcissel's life history as a classic r-selected strategy among temperate songbirds.
